subtopic: WELCOME EXTENDED ON RETURN TO THE HOUSE FROM LONDON CONFERENCE

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the opposition):
subtopic: WELCOME EXTENDED ON RETURN TO THE HOUSE FROM LONDON CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not often in the history of a leader of an opposition that he can speak on behalf of the whole parliament in which he sits, and at the same time be reasonably sure of unanimous support for what he says. I feel in this particular instance, however, that I am in that position.
Because of the war and the serious matters connected with it, there is not much time left for pleasant occasions such as that which is afforded now to members of this house. Therefore this occasion stands out in bold relief; because after nearly four full and very strenuous weeks in which the Prime Minister has dealt with important commonwealth, international and war-time business for Canada overseas, he has returned to our midst, again to take his part in the affairs of parliament.
One of my words at this time should be an-expression of gratitude and appreciation to His Majesty, to the Prime Minister of Great Britain, to the members of the United Kingdom cabinet, to the members of the House of Lords and the House of Commons at Westminster-indeed to the entire people of Great Britain-for the spontaneous and open-hearted welcome they extended to our Prime Minister while he was there, a welcome which we in turn, as a nation of Canadian citizens, are pleased to share.
The general tone of the welcome the Prime Minister of Canada received in that overseas domain was an indication of how the nation he represents is held over there. I fancy the gesture of good will and affection extended to the Prime Minister on behalf of himself and the people of Canada will remain long with him as a treasured and prized memory, as it will for the rest of us in Canada who share it with him.
May I say this to the Prime Minister: We are glad you are back. We are glad your journey was a safe one, and that you have been able to maintain and to preserve that measure of good health in which you left and which, apparently, is unabated on your return. We hope, too, that in the near future we shall be able to welcome two other leaders from the sister dominions of Australia and New Zealand. We shall welcome them not only on their own account, but because of the splendid achievements of their respective nations, both
Welcome to Prime Minister

in war and in peace. They stand high in the esteem, the admiration and the affection of the Canadian people, and I think it well that we pay this public tribute to them.
And so, if I may, on behalf of the members [DOT]of the house, I extend to the Prime Minister the very warmest and most cordial of welcomes upon his return, and I say to him: We are happy indeed to have you with us once more.

We feel, as I think all the house feels,

We feel it is a cause of satisfaction that he was able to make the trip safely, over there and back, and we shall be glad indeed to see him ready again to take his part in the government *of the country.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WELCOME EXTENDED ON RETURN TO THE HOUSE FROM LONDON CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I am sure you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members will not be surprised when I say that it is with great difficulty I find words wherewith to express my appreciation of the welcome extended to me this afternoon, as I return to my duties in the House of Commons.
May I say to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr, Graydon) that it was particularly pleasing to be welcomed by him, both as an old friend and as leader of the opposition in the house. There are times when, I imagine, my hon. friend would not welcome my return as cordially as he has this afternoon. But may I say to him that I have never come into the House of Commons at any time when I found myself more *pleased with having that opportunity. I thank him for the exceedingly generous and felicitous way in which he has extended a welcome on behalf of his party, and I thank too, my hon. friends, the leaders of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and the Social Credit parties for the equally felicitous and generous manner in which they have extended their good wishes, and those of their t{Mr. Graydon.]
followers. I shall ever remember with gratitude as well as pride, the welcome accorded from all sides of the house.
May I say to all hon. members that at no time have I been insensible of the burden of responsibility which was mine. If I have been fortunate enough not to disappoint too greatly any hopes or expectations they may have been kind enough to entertain of my representation of this House of Commons in Great Britain, I cannot be too grateful. The welcome which I received in Britain, which as my hon. friend the leader of the opposition quite rightly says was a welcome of the entire people of Britain, from their majesties the king and queen to those engaged in humble but essential tasks in that country at this time was certainly a welcome to the representative of the people of Canada and an expression of the feeling of the heart and mind of Britain toward the Canadian people. My visit afforded me an opportunity to realize how deeply the people of the United Kingdom feel toward the people of Canada. No words could begin to acknowledge the expressions that came from all sides as to the war effort of our country, and what it meant to have Canada and the other self-governing nations of the commonwealth represented at the side of the British government and people, at this of all times in the history of the world.
Had time permitted, and had I not just concluded a journey of over four thousand miles in one day and night, I should have liked to say something to the house of the many impressions gathered while in the United Kingdom, but doubtless I will have other opportunities for doing so. I shall accordingly make but a reference or two to those impressions. First, I should like to say that I think the conference in every way was a very great success, not only in what it. disclosed of unity of purpose, unity of feeling and unity of action on the part of all who were there, but also in what it represented, in a symbolic way, to other parts of the world of the complete unity of the British commonwealth of nations and their high purpose at this time. It would not be possible to overestimate the value which the discussions at the conference were to all present. We had the privilege, the very great privilege, of having the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Mr. Churchill, preside over practically all the meetings. It was an inspiration to have his leadership. I am sure hon. members will be pleased to know that the Prime Minister of Great Britain was never in better health and never displayed more vigour than at the present time. During the last few

Welcome to Prime Minister
years I have seen him on many occasions; at Washington, here in Ottawa and also in Britain, but I can say that I do not recall ever having seen Mr. Churchill display the vigour, the energy, the tirelessness and the utter freedom from fatigue that he displayed throughout the entire conference. This means a great deal to all of us.
The discussions were free, frank and friendly. I could not honestly say that there were material differences between us on any questions. There were shades of opinion; there were points of view that were perhaps different, arising out of the different geographical positions of the different nations of the commonwealth, and the local situations they must necessarily take into account, but there was no difficulty whatever in arriving at a convergence of view with respect to all matters that were discussed. The programme itself was very full. It covered a variety of subjects, dealing of course primarily with matters of defence, with plans of the whole war, but dealing also with questions of foreign policy, matters related to the period of transition, to post-war reconstruction, and to the fashioning of a new world order. In the nature of things the proceedings of the conference were very secret, and one has to be doubly careful at this moment to disclose very little of what took place within its secret councils. These are moments when the enemy is more active than he has been at any time. He would be quick to piece together remarks that might be made in different parts of the world as to what had taken place, and turn them to his own advantage. But I can say, and I am proud to say, that its entire proceedings were marked by a degree of unanimity and determination that it would be impossible to exaggerate.
I believe the house would be interested were I to give just a line which might come to hon. members as from Mr. Churchill himself, for it, better than anything else I can think of, describes wThat the conference meant not only to him but to all of us who were present from the other nations of the commonwealth. I give the words as spoken by the Prime Minister at the opening of the concluding session, at the time the representatives signed the declaration which was subsequently published. Mr. Churchill said:
We have found comfort in hours of stress and anxiety. In days when great military operations are proceeding with vigour, and, at last, not uncheered by hopes of success, we have found pleasure in meeting men whose companionship is .a comfort, whose comradeship is strong as a rock. . . . My confidence in the future is enormously strengthened by all that lias passed around this council board, and I am sure that
this meeting will in future years be looked back to as one of the important milestones in the history of our united association.
My hon. friends have been kind enough to make reference to my part in the proceedings. May I say to them and to other hon. members of the house that, if it was in any way satisfactory, that was due to the circumstance that I had the privilege of giving expression to what I believe to be feelings and sentiments which are held in common throughout this dominion. I sought to avoid' making reference to matters which might represent differences of opinion on any question.. The things that we all hold in common are so much greater than the things that divide us-that it was not difficult for me to feel that, when I spoke, I was speaking not for any particular party, not for either side of the-house, but for members of all parties in this House of Commons and for the people of Canada as a whole.
My stay in Britain over the past three weeks and more has permitted me to gain exceptional information from the inside, from those-who know more about the position of affairs-in Europe and throughout the world than-any other men; to obtain information from-those in the highest positions on the military side as well as from those in the highest positions on the civil side. I have been permitted, also, to see something of the tremendous developments that have taken place in preparation for the final great task which may come at any moment. As a result of what I have seen and heard, I feel more reassured than I have felt at any time as to the certainty of ultimate victory. But may I say also that I feel more deeply than ever that the struggle is going to be very much greater and more difficult than any of -us begin to comprehend!.
I believe it is going to be longer than perhaps most of us imagine. As to its being a difficult struggle, a hard and severe struggle, a stupendous struggle, there -can be no doubt. It will be the greatest conflict in arms that has ever taken place in the history of the world. We must be prepared, all of us, everywhere, to hear from time to time of situations that may cause us, for the moment, great concern. But let me say to the people of Canada, when that moment comes, have nodoubt whatever as to what the ultimate outcome of the struggle will be, for I believe, knowing the plans of the united nations and what is being done to give effect to them, that there can be no question at all as to what the ultimate outcome will be.
I should like to add a further word as a result of what I have heard and seen- and felt. I do not believe that this war is going to end
Welcome to Prime Minister

the conflict between the different classes and races of men. The enemy of to-day must be completely destroyed, but forces of evil have been let loose in this world which it is going to be difficult indeed to bring to bay. These forces of evil are going to continue to destroy much of what is best in the world, for many *days, I am afraid, possibly years, after the main struggle is over. In all of our deliberations here, as I am sure will be the case in the deliberations of all other assemblies of free nations, we must never lose sight of the fact that our greatest work may still lie ahead in seeking to trample under foot and slay the dragon that to-day is seeking to destroy humanity itself.
I have been impressed more than ever with the truth that Britain holds the gates of freedom for the world. She has carried a great burden through the years, almost through centuries, in keeping open those gates of freedom. She has been hard pressed, very hard pressed in recent years in keeping those gates ajar. I believe that if the nations of the commonwealth had not found it possible in their hearts, from aheir love of freedom and sense of justice, to *come immediately as they did to the side of Britain when this great struggle broke out, she herself might not have found it possible to keep those gates open. If those gates are * ever closed there will be no more freedom for men in this world, I believe, for a thousand .years to come. So I say that our task should :go beyond this war and that we must continue tto share with all freedom-loving peoples the igitaat task of keeping those gates of freedom, which Britain represents, open to mankind.
I should add that I never was so proud of Canada as I was in Britain when I saw what our armed forces meant to the people there, and what they are accomplishing. It was not my privilege, obviously, to witness our naval forces in action, though events took place at the time of my visit which caused us all to realize their service and sacrifice as perhaps they have not been recognized at any other moment. But I did have the privilege of [DOT]visiting our bomber group at one or two of its stations and of seeing something of the army and of its extent and work. I felt a pride in Canada's effort greater than any I have ' hitherto known or expressed. On some other *occasion I shall have a chance to say a word about that and about the work people on the farms and in industries in Canada are doing to keep Britain supplied with the food and the war materials she so greatly needs.
Let me conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that I was never more proud to be a Canaj
dian than I am at this hour, and I was never more proud to be a citizen of the British commonwealth.

2.	The reparation payments were not paid under any particular heading of the treaty of peace, since under article 232 compensation may be claimed from Germany in respect of damages under the following categories:
(1)	Damage to injured persons and to surviving dependents by personal injury to or death of civilians caused by acts of war, including bombardments or other attacks on land, on sea, or from the air, and all the direct consequences thereof, and of all operations of war by the two groups of belligerents wherever arising.

allies in their own territory or in occupied or invaded territory to civilian victims of all acts injurious to health or capacity to work, or to honour, as well as to the surviving dependents of such victims.
(4)	Damage caused by any kind of maltreatment of prisoners of war.
(5)	As damage caused to the peoples of the allied and associated powers, all pensions and compensation in the nature of pensions to naval and military victims of war (including members of the air forces), whether mutilated, wounded, sick or invalided, and to the dependents of such victims, the amount due to the allied and associated governments being calculated for each of them as being the capitalized cost of such pensions and compensation at the date of the coming into force of the present treaty, on the basis of the scales in force in France at such date.
(6)	The cost of assistance by the governments of the allied and associated powers to prisoners of war and to their families and dependents.
(7)	Allowances by the governments of the allied and associated powers to the families and dependents of mobilized persons or persons serving with the forces, the amount due to them for each calendar year in which hostilities occurred being calculated for each

government on the basis of the average scale for such payments in force in France during that year.
(8)	Damage caused to civilians by being forced by Germany or her allies to labour without just remuneration.
(9)	Damage in respect of all property wherever situated belonging to any of the allied or associated states or their nationals, with the exception of naval and military works or materials, which has been carried off, seized, injured or destroyed by the acts of Germany or her allies on land, on sea or from the air, or damaged directly in consequence of hostilities or or any operations of war.
(10)	Damage in the form of levies, fines and other similar exactions imposed by Germany or her allies upon the civilian population, and the total amount paid represented an insignificant percentage of the cost to Canada under the above ten headings.

That it is expedient to bring in .a measure to provide regulations enabling persons (to
Prime Ministers' Conference

be described as Canadian war service electors) to exercise their franchise and the Canadian prisoners of war to vote toy proxy at any general election held during the present war; and also to provide amendments to the Dominion Elections Act, 1938, consequential to such regulations; and to provide further that any expenses incurred in the carrying out of the said measure shall be paid out of unappropriated moneys in the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.

speechtext:
I have a question to direct
to the Prime Minister. Perhaps I should preface it by saying that in his absence an inquiry was directed to the acting leader of the government with respect to the prospective visits of the Prime Ministers of Australia and New Zealand. The acting leader of the government at that time was not in possession of full information with respect to the details of the projected visit, but indicated to the house that the invitation extended by the Prime Minister to the Prime Ministers of Australia and New Zealand had been accepted. Is the Prime Minister now in a position to give us any information with respect to the visits of these two prominent gentlemen?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: VISIT TO CANADA OF PRIME MINISTERS OF AUSTRALIA AND NEW ZEALAND
speechtext: I am happy to say to my hon. friend that both Mr. Curtin, Prime Minister of Australia, and Mr. Fraser, Prime Minister of New Zealand, intimated to me that they were much looking forward to being in Canada in the course of the next few days, or at latest the next few weeks-they were not quite certain as to the particular date at which they would leave London. I rather expect that Mr. Curtin will be here very soon, and Mr. Fraser immediately after. I should like to say to the house that I mentioned to Field Marshal Smuts how delighted we would be if he could find it possible to visit Canada at this time, but his house is in session and he will be returning to South Africa. The other gentlemen are each fortunate in having concluded a session.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID-FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, May 19, consideration in committee of a resolution to [DOT]

War Appropriation-Agriculture
grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Agricultural supplies board-administration, $51,300.

This appropriation calls for 151,300 for the administration of the agricultural supplies board, which was set up, I understand, in September, 1939, under order in council P.C. 2621. The duties of the board are clearly set out in the order in council. They are very wide and comprehensive. There are a number of them, but I think I should place on Hansard the first duty of the board as it is laid down in the order in council:
To direct and regulate through the various dominion and provincial agricultural services and through advisory boards representative of the industry which are already constituted or which may be established, the production, preparation and conservation of farm products.
A little farther down it gives the board power:
Subject to the approval of the governor in council; to deal with matters pertaining to the purchase of agricultural products.
I believe that opens up in a general way the whole question of agricultural production and of the collection, processing and marketing of farm products. I should like therefore to take this opportunity to deal for a few moments-and a few moments only

with the agricultural situation in Canada as I see it. It is true that these estimates relate closely to the civil estimates, some of which have already been discussed. It is however very difficult, as I pointed out when the civil estimates were first being discussed, to separate the two; therefore if in the course of my remarks there may be some overlapping or some repetition I am sure that the committee and the minister will consider that it is unavoidable.
I believe that everyone in Canada, and particularly the farming population, should view with a good deal of pride the high level which our agricultural production has reached. There has been a steady increase in that production each year since the war began. On several occasions the Minister of Agriculture has presented figures to the house showing this to be true. I think it is only fair to say that in the course of his remarks he has sought to give credit for that increase in production to the Department of Agriculture and to the government generally. In doing so he has been backed up more than once by hon. members on the government benches,
who have from time to time sought to attribute the increase in agricultural production to the minister's activities and to government policy.
When the civil estimates were before the committee on February 18, I recall that the hon. member for Moose Jaw, the hon. member for Macdonald and the hon. member for Brant made statement to the effect that this increase in agricultural production was largely due to government policy. In fact, their remarks were so flattering that I could not help thinking that a parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture may be appointed at some future time and hon. members were vying with each other as to who would have the best chance of getting the position.
Too many applicants.

The second difficulty under which the farmers have been labouring ever since the war began is that of insufficient prices. I will admit immediately that prices are somewhat more favourable to-day than they were at the beginning of the war, but there has been and there is still an improper relationship between the prices of the farmer's products and the prices of the goods and services that he has to buy. This is due in no small measure to the policy of the government and to their attitude with regard to the price ceiling and the application of this price ceiling not only to farm commodities but to what the farmer has to buy. The lack of parity between farm prices and other prices results from the wrong foundation laid by the wartime prices and trade board when price ceilings were established. No one will deny that the price of farm products went out of line with other prices during that period. The period chosen was October 15 to November 11, 1941. The price ceilings have been calculated on that basis ever since; therefore the farmer has been at a decided disadvantage so far as the price structure is concerned.
The third difficulty I should like to mention is that of labour shortage on the farm. It is true that the farmer's efficiency has been greatly enhanced by the increased use of power machinery, but here the farmer has again been at a disadvantage because often he has not been able to procure the machinery he needs. There has been a dearth of supply. Sometimes priorities have been to blame. It is an open secret among the farmers of Ontario that they have not been able to purchase the supplies that would have been available from the United States because of government and board interference.
No one will deny that there has been a labour shortage; it still exists. Just the other day I read in one of the labour reviews that between March 1939 and March 1943 over 100,000 men had left the farms to go into the army, the navy and the air force, and over 250,000 men had left the farms to go into industry of all kinds. In spite of this drain, however, agricultural production in Canada is some thirty per cent higher than it was in 1939. It is interesting to note that agricultural production per worker in Canada is over fifty per cent higher than it was in 1939, owing, of course, partly to the bountiful harvest which we have had, but as well to the increased labour of the farmer. This increase in agricultural production has been brought about often at great sacrifice, not only on the part of the farmer himself, but

on the part of his wife and family who have perhaps done from time to time more than their share.
Another factor in the labour situation is the increased cost of labour on the farm. I have already mentioned that the prices of agricultural products are somewhat higher than they were at the beginning of the war; but it is also true that the price of labour on the farm has gone up to a far greater extent than the price of farm products. To-day labour on the farm, when it can be found, is enjoying wages twice and sometimes three times as high as it was before the war began.
I have often wondered why it is that farmers are expected to carry on and to prosper without a fair share of the national income. I have often heard it said that if farmers were to keep books as other industries do, and provide for depreciation, repairs, wages and all other incidentals, they would never put a plough into the ground because they could never show a profit. That fact is all the more deplorable, because Canada, with her vast agricultural areas, is and must continue to be an agricultural country. Prosperity of the farmers is the key to national prosperity. I believe that is a statement with which everyone will agree, particularly in a country such as this. Therefore too great consideration cannot be given, in any scheme for reconstruction, to the welfare of agriculture.
Another disturbing consideration in our national economy is the fact that although agriculture is so important, our farm population is gradually declining. As we look at the census figures for different decades we find there has been a steady decrease. The 1941 census shows 45 per cent of our population classed as rural, but of that percentage only 27J per cent consists purely of those who are on the farms and are classed as farmers. The other 18 per cent is vitally interested in and closely connected with agriculture, of course. The 55 per cent who are not at all classed as rural are also vitally interested in the farmer's prosperity.
In 1940 our capital investment in agriculture in Canada amounted to about four and a half billions of dollars, made up of land, buildings, equipment, and live stock. The outlay of the farmers for building materials, equipment and repairs affects to a great extent the welfare of all the people. Everybody is vitally interested in the ability of the farmer to spend. The other day I found a paragraph in the report of the advisory committee on reconstruction, dealing with agricultural policy,

War Appropriation-Agriculture
which I believe would be of interest to hon. members. This is what I find at page 8, relating to volume of business:
Closely related both to the number of persons engaged in agriculture and to the capital investment in the industry is the volume of business, or the proceeds from the employment of labour and capital. In 1942 the gross value of Canadian agricultural production was $2-1 billion. Of more significance, however, is the cash income from the sale of that portion of the output that eventually reaches the market. This figure, $1-1 billion, represents the amount the farmers of Canada had to pay their hired help, maintain or improve their plant and equipment, pay taxes, and provide for the well-being and education of their families. Most of this money is spent immediately-much of it, in fact, was actually spent before it was received-and its contribution to rural and urban development is both direct and significant.
I read that because I believe it bears out what I have been trying to convey to the house, namely, that upon the prosperity of the farmer depends the prosperity of a country such as Canada.
When the Minister of Finance spoke, closing the debate on the Bank Act, he mentioned that there have been in Canada cycles of prosperity and of depression. This is true, and it is a condition which I believe will always remain. It is unfortunate however that the farmer is usually the first and greatest victim of depressions. In support of that contention I point to a fact which in my opinion is important. Distribution of national income varies as between times of prosperity and times of depression. When we compare the farmers' share of the national income in the basic year 1926, which is often used as a basis for comparison, with the farmers' share of income in depression years, we find that during the depression, farmers' income was only 45 per cent of the share which they held in 1926.	.
If we take the group of salary and wage earners we find that the share of the national income they enjoyed in the depression years amounted to 91-6 per cent of that enjoyed in good years. The investment income group were even better, at 94 per cent. It is clear therefore that during depression years the farmers' share of income dropped 56 per cent, while that of other groups dropped only six per cent or nine per cent. I believe this condition is to a great extent responsible for lengthy depressions. When the farmer cannot purchase consumer goods the result is unemployment of other groups in the community. There is no doubt in my mind that the purchasing power of the farmer cannot be as effective as it should be until a proper relationship is developed between agricultural income and the income enjoyed by other groups. Despite any increase there may
be in farm prices, and despite what may be contended by members of the government, that relationship is not satisfactory to-day. And if we need any proof we need only look at an item further down in the estimates where we see the government has provided $47,000,000 for farm subsidies.
After the price ceilings were established in 1939 it was very soon found either that the ceilings must be changed or prices to the farmers must be supplemented. The government-the wartime prices and trade board, or whoever was responsible-decided to provide subsidies. For some time those subsidies were meted out by the Commodity Prices Stabilization corporation. Last year-I believe it was either May or June-a change was made, and this work was given over to the agricultural food board. The minister might very well explain why the change was made. Although I have no doubt he has a good reason for it, I should like to know what the reason is.
I have already pointed out that, in the last census, farmers constituted some 27i per cent of the population. But their percentage of national income was much lower than that. Figures received recently from the bureau of statistics show that despite their percentage of population, in the four war years the farmers' share of national income amounts to only 13-4 to 14-5 per cent. I cannot use the figures for 1943, because they are only estimated, and I have been asked not to use them. But if we take the figures for 1942 they show that the national income was some seven and a half billions of dollars. Of that amount the farmers' share was $1,084,000,000 or 14-5 per cent. If we add to that the whole $47,000,000 provided in the estimates for farm subsidies, we find that farmers' income amounts to only about fifteen per cent of the total income. I want to emphasize as strongly as I can the need for some action which will provide more equitable distribution of the national income as between agricultural and other groups.
Farmers are looking forward with a good deal of hope and expectation to the action announced by the government in the speech from the throne to provide floor prices for agricultural products. In the past it has been the practice to accept the consumer price as the basis for the farmers' price structure. From the consumer price must be deducted profits of the retailer, the wholesaler, the processor and the collectors of farm produce. The farmer -the primary producer-has had to take what is left.
In support of the point I am making I wish to refer to a statement made by Mr. Stanley McLean, head of Canada Packers. When he
War Appropriation-Agriculture

appeared before the price spreads committee he bore that statement out to the full. It seems to me the time has come when the system should be entirely reversed. In my judgment there should be a producer price based upon the cost of efficient production. The profits of middlemen, such as collectors, processors and distributors, should be sufficiently liberal to provide an incentive for them to operate, because we must have them to process and distribute our goods, but I believe there should be government interference if their profits are exorbitant or there is evidence of speculation so that they exploit either the producer or the consumer.
As we go through the estimates I shall have an opportunity to discuss other matters, but at the moment I want to discuss just one point which I have -mentioned to the house more than once previously. I refer to the personnel of the various boards which have been set up and which come under this item. I have in mind the agricultural supplies board; the meat board, formerly known as the bacon board; the special products board; the agricultural food board, and the dairy board. In addition we have two other boards which from time to time have dealt with farm products as to prices and so on; that is, the wartime prices and trade board and the commodity prices stabilization board. All these boards deal with agricultural matters, but I am sorry to say that there is not a representative of agriculture or a primary producer on one of them. On the meat board we have a representative of the packers and a representative of the transportation companies. There are no producers on the dairy board, but there is a representative of the distributors and a representative of the shippers. I have brought up this matter on a number of occasions. I presume the minister's answer will be, as it has been in the past, that the government have set up advisory boards on which there is producer representation, but none of these advisory boards has any power. They may be consulted by the other boards, but I have heard it said that very often decisions are reached and policies enunciated and then sent to the advisory boards for their consideration, after the thing has been done.
I am not bringing up this matter in order to criticize, but the farmers feel very keenly indeed the fact that there is no producer representation on these boards, which are composed principally of members of the Department of Agriculture. All these boards are more or less interlocking; that is, you may find one man on two or three of them. These are estimable gentlemen, and I do not want to find any fault with them. I know they are IMr. Senn.]
industrious, capable and honest, but I do not believe any of them is a primary producer, and I think they might very easily get a different viewpoint if they had some producer representation on these boards. Once more I appeal to the minister to change his policy in this regard. For his own sake, for the benefit of agriculture, and in order to put farmers in a better frame of mind, he should see to it that there is producer representation on these boards.

Mr. Chairman, since we are on agricultural appropriations and production, I renew my request for full and final exemption for farmers from military service. Who could estimate the amount spent in travelling expenses and the time lost by farmers because of the way the Mobilization Act is presently enforced? Why insist on medical re-examinations when the family doctors have already categorized the men who have been called up? Is it reasonable or fair, Mr. Chairman, thus to belittle the undeniable qualifications of the civilian physicians and the service they have rendered their country? I say it is an uncalled for insult to men who have devoted their time and made sacrifices for the government and the Canadian people.
As for the agricultural situation in Canada, it is becoming more and more alarming. The lack of market for hogs and other meat cattle, added to the scarcity of farm help, during the last few months, have created an unbearable situation. Ask the farmer who has sold hogs and beef cattle since last fall what treatment he has received at the hands of Canada Packers and other similar trusts, whom the government should bring to their senses.
All the necessary powers are vested in the ministry to guard our farmers from those heartless firms, who have been taking advantage of them and swindling them for so many years. The government and the trusts have to take the blame for the spoilage of millions of pounds of meat, while our civilians were rationed and large families and young children were suffering from hunger. I urge the government to see that such a deplorable state of affairs never recurs as it is a shame for our country. That is all.

I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of the hon. member for Haldimand in regard to agriculture in this country, and I concur in many of the things he said. However, I felt that the effectiveness of his speech was somewhat lost when I remembered that he was a member of this house from 1931 to 1935; that his party was in power in those years and he was chairman

War Appropriation-Agriculture
of the agriculture committee, and that during this period agriculture received the lowest share of the national income that,.it has ever received in Canada's history.
To what party did you belong?

The party to which I still belong. As a matter of fact at that time I believe agriculture received less than nine per cent of the national income. Even to-day we are not getting our fair share of the national income, but still we are a great deal better off than we were during the years I have mentioned. I think that deeds count for more than words when it comes to endeavouring to improve the position of agriculture. I do not propose to follow the remarks of the hon. member, but I should like to pay a compliment to the producers of this country for the way in which they have increased production under great difficulties, particularly in regard to the amount of labour that has been available to them. When you consider the number of men who have gone from agriculture, and consider further what agriculture has been able to do during this war period, the record is a remarkable one.
I should like to draw the minister's attention to the matter of increasing the supply of farm implements. In the agriculture committee last year we were promised that there would be a considerable increase in the amount of farm equipment made available during this year. That increase has not come about as yet, at least from information I have received from western Canada; they are in an even worse position than last year in regard to the number of new implements available. I believe the minister would do well to bring this matter to the attention of the departments that have the responsibility for seeing that the necessary release is made of steel and other raw materials required in the manufacture of agricultural implements.
With respect to coarse grains, I believe they should be handled entirely through the wheat board. Last year the wheat board took over complete control of the handling of wheat and flax, which was taken entirely out of the hands of the speculative market. But this has not been done with coarse grains and the result is that the government has had to pass a number of regulations to control and direct the people who are at present handling coarse grains in Canada. It has been a bigger headache to the wheat board than if they had been handling the whole thing themselves, both as regards making coarse grains available to feeders in eastern Canada and as regards exports. I see no reason why all oui grain should not be handled entirely
through the wheat board. I think it would be to the advantage of everyone concerned. But apparently the government is determined to keep a nucleus of the Winnipeg grain exchange alive so that it may again start to function as soon as the war is over. I see no other reason why coarse grains and rye should have been left under the present setup. I know that the farmers of western Canada are firmly convinced that the speculative market in Winnipeg should be got rid of at the earliest possible moment. It is pretty hard to convince them that the selling of their crop six or seven times over on the speculative market adds one more bushel to it or changes its quality whatsoever, and it is equally hard to convince the consumers that because the grain has been handled several times on the Winnipeg market the price of bread is thereby decreased. Certainly everything that is taken out of the price of the grain between leaving the farmer and reaching the consumer comes out of either the producer or the consumer. We believe that that spread could be recouped if the grain were handled through the wheat board.
Another matter I would bring to the minister's attention has to do with the rebate on feed grains. At present in western Canada men who are engaged in the feed business but who do. not operate a farm are able to obtain a rebate of 10 cents a bushel on oats, 15 cents a bushel on barley and 25 cents a bushel on wheat for feeding purposes. The minister in reply to a question by the hon. member for Selkirk, said, when his estimates were before the committee last, that the government was not particularly interested in the people who were operating feeding lots.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: I am sure that my hon. friend does not want to misrepresent the situation. There are no rebates paid to people who feed grain. There is an extra amount paid to the farmer who delivers to the elevator.
The man who buys it from the elevator gets a rebate of 10 cents.

No, the man who buys it from the elevator buys it at the ceiling price, but the man who sells the grain gets an extra 10 cents on oats and an extra 15 cents on barley. There is no rebate for the person who buys it.

It amounts to that so far as the farmer who is feeding the grain is concerned, because he feeds that grain at the ceiling price plus 10 or 15 or 25 cents a bushel as the case may be. It means that the man
War Appropriation-Agriculture

who is operating a feeding lot and is feeding the grain gets it cheaper than the producer who is feeding the grain.

There are costs in
connection with it that have to be taken into consideration-costs, for instance, in moving the grain from one place to another, as against feeding it right on the farm.
But the farmer has to pay those costs in delivering the grain to the elevator.
The farmer who purchases it to feed pays just as much as the other in getting it moved to his farm.

I think that has now
been corrected.

I hope it has been. I know there were many complaints about it. It was a condition which should not have been allowed to exist. I know it existed three months ago. At that time I had one particular complaint with respect to it. Apparently these milling companies, because they are subsidized in the price they are paying for wheat, are making a nice profit on the handling of flour and they were forcing their dealers to take flour in order to obtain their feed.
There are several other matters which I wish to bring to the attention of the minister, but I will do so as the individual items are taken up.

In any discussion generally on the question of agriculture and its place in Canada, it is necessary for us to consider and agree that food production as it exists at present must be maintained for the period of the war, and that possibly food increases will be necessary after the war. This premise is necessary first of all for the projects we contemplate through our work on UNRRA and also for the fullest inplementation of the section of the Atlantic charter which deals with the freedom of the people of the world from want. It is a fine thing for those of us who for several years have lived in agricultural parts of Canada, particularly the west, to realize that food has become such a powerful weapon of the united nations. At the present time it is one of the most important weapons in their arsenals, though it may be almost a paradox that while most weapons of war are death-dealing, food as a weapon in this war is a means of sustaining [DOT]life.	.
Not only must we step up our programme of food production for the purposes of the war, but Canada's agricultural policy must be much more far-reaching. During the Hot Springs conference, when it was decided to set up an interim commission and to have one representative from each of the forty-four nations to draft a constitution for a permanent food organization, Canada was recognized among the nations as having a great part to play. Mr. L. B. Pearson, who was one of the members of the important committee on supply of UNRRA, writing in Canadian Affairs magazine, April 1, 1944, said this:
Peace sits uneasily on an empty stomach. . . . When the United States and United Kingdom governments decided some time ago that the united nations should begin the process of organizing for peace, they did not convoke an assembly to discuss general political or economic matters. The first united nations conference in May 1943 at Hot Springs dealt with one question only, and an essentially practical one, "Food and agriculture." Hence the first permanent united nations organization set up in the world will likely be that on food and agriculture, now being worked out in Washington by the interim committee representing the forty-four nations.
It would appear that in the past wars have been mostly of a destructive nature. Possibly this war is different from all others which have preceded it in that it is producing more new and constructive types of thinking. One of the most constructive lines of thought which are being developed concerns this question of cooperation of peoples after the war, to see that the want which prior to this war had devastated such large regions of the earth shall never again prevail. In other words there will be a great impulse to further cooperation among the nations. I am glad to see that our own government is giving a constructive lead on this particular question. I do not like always to quote from United States authorities on this subject, and I am glad to be able to cite the words of Doctor Barton, our own deputy minister of agriculture. In a statement to the press which was reproduced in the Ottawa Citizen on June 2, 1943, he is reported from Washington as follows:
Canada will be required to increase food production, not only in the immediate post-war period, but in the years to follow, if the recommendations of the united nations food conference are carried into effect.
Doctor Barton continued:
The whole picture, as it has been developed here, should appeal to Canada because it is one of expanding agricultural economy.
The deputy minister went on to say that in the period of shortages immediately after the war there will be need for orderly marketing through some form of international arrangement and, even in the long-range view, it may
War Appropriation-Agriculture

'be necessary for some farm products. "To that end," he continued, "we may have to join with others in recognizing that some form of cooperative production may be required."
In viewing the vast perspective which now opens up before us in this new era of peaceful development which we believe will be possible after the war, two things stand out in my mind most clearly. First of all, food production must be increased according to this country's ability to produce certain types of food more cheaply than other countries can produce them, in the first place for the immediate purpose of present war needs and for relief schemes; and secondly, food increases must be maintained and absorbed to a far greater degree than before by our own population through gradually achieving higher standards of living.	*
Canada's farm requirements, we must recognize, have depended in the past upon the income of her people, but food requirements are not like other things. They are a basic necessity for the life and health of the nation, and we should not judge food by the ability of the people to pay for it; we should judge the quantity of food needed by the accepted standard necessary for health. In 1940 the average consumption of food in Canada was roughly 1,038 pounds per year per person. That was a fairly high average, taking into consideration the food consumption of other peoples of the world. But without doubt we must realize that numbers of our own people could to their great advantage increase the amount and quality of the food they eat.
In certain surveys made in Canada just prior to the war, I think we can find evidence enough to prove that a larger consumption of food in this country is still a desirable thing. Studies made just before the war among numbers of families in the country show that when the average income was anywhere from $1,000 to $2,000 per annum, these families used an appreciably larger amount of protective foods than did those families whose income was below $1,000 per annum. Those who received from $1,000 to $2,000 used on an average 12 per cent more meat, 10 per cent more milk, 10 per cent more eggs, 7 per cent more fish and a larger amount of vegetables, fruit and butter than those who received less than $1,000 a year. These same studies would indicate that the more *well-to-do families whose income was anywhere above $4,000 a year ate far more of the nutritionally important foods which give the human body a greater fighting chance to resist infection and disease. This income group, receiving over $4,000 a year, ate 50 per cent more fish, 34 per cent more meat, 38 per cent more
tMrs. Nielsen.]
milk, 15 per cent more eggs and a proportionately larger amount of fruit, vegetables and butter than families earning less than $1,000 a year.
The point is that if the people of Canada were able to procure the amount of food which it is necessary for them to have for their health, we should need more food than we were having prior to the war for our own home market. The same Canadian council on nutrition stated, that in order to bring the adequate level of nutrition of all Canadian families up to the desired point, we would need roughly 1,500,000,000 pounds of food a year in the form of milk, eggs, meat, vegetables, dried beans, small fruits and things of that kind.
It is all very well to speak of Canada, and Canada of course is of greatest importance to us when it comes to the welfare of our people. But we must recognize that our own standards are very much better than those of many others in the world. If you come to consider the question as it affects some of the other nations, you realize what scope there is for the increase of food production if we are to implement those clauses of the Atlantic charter which declare that no people should suffer from want. The report from the mixed committee of the League of Nations before the war showed that in the countries with the largest surplus of food, such as Canada and the United States, there was still a considerable amount of malnutrition, but it was nothing in comparison with the conditions that prevailed in India and China. Take one food product, such as milk. In Canada there are three or four people dependent on the milk of one cow, whereas in China there are roughly fifty thousand people to every cow. This will give some indication of the need for an increase in live stock if we are to supply the needs of the people of the world to give them the health conditions to which they are entitled.
In normal times it is estimated that in China about 8,000,000 people die of malnutrition every year, and in India the condition is similar. Diet deficiencies are causing infant mortality, blindness, crippling of children, and this condition is widely prevalent among India's 400,000,000. In the last disastrous famine in India, roughly 1,000,000 people died from malnutrition. In Africa, Mexico, South America, Egypt, and in other parts of the world you find malnutrition and diseases resulting from diet deficiencies. Estimates made by the same committee of the League of Nations show that of the 2,100,000,000 people of the world, roughly two-thirds, or 1,400.000,000, have always eaten diets consisting of

War Appropriation-Agriculture
about eighty per cent of cereals and potatoes, though the health authorities say that a good diet should contain only about twenty-one per cent of cereals and potatoes, the rest being made up of protective foods.
If peace can be maintained with some degree of security after the war by the continued collaboration of the nations of the world it will make a great difference to the ability of many countries to grow food. For instance, many of the countries of Europe, if they were freed from war, or at any rate from the fear of war, would be able to reduce certain of their cereal crops ajid animal products which before the war they insisted on producing in their effort to be self-sufficient. If in the future they are not in fear of war they will cease to grow these things and buy them from countries like Canada which can produce them more cheaply, and in Europe the farmers will concentrate to a far greater degree upon the production of such things as milk, eggs, fruit and vegetables, so that their own diet will be of a greater variety. That will add greatly to the ability, of the farmers of this country to continue the exports of food which they can grow. Therefore a great deal of the agricultural problem of the world depends upon the ability of the united nations to collaborate in trade agreements whereby those who can produce certain types of food shall be encouraged in such production, and whereby free trade with other countries who are producing types of food different from those produced at home will bring about better results.
It becomes very clear to all of us that if the people of the world are to be free from want, if we are to see that food is available for all, it will be necessary for us to ensure that people are in a position to buy food. That of course is the other part of the problem. There must be employment. There must be increased industrial production and there must be free international trade. We can remove the devastation of poverty and hunger from the world only if we see that certain selfish interests and political prejudices no longer are in a position to deny to the people of the world their free access to food. I think we should all back up the statement which was made a while ago by the vice president of the United States of America, Mr. Wallace. He said:
Whenever these forces, of special privilege and international monopoly are found, our job is to fight them.
For surely the winning of the peace is bound up with the regulation of food supplies to the peoples of the world.
The agricultural workers of Canada have done remarkable things during this war to increase production. I think that all of us who come from agricultural constituencies have a great deal of pride in the fact that with their limited supplies of man-power, and with women and children having to help out considerably in the fields and during harvest time, the farmers have increased the food production roughly by about forty per cent.
Farming, of course, is not like industry. It is not possible to regulate farming on such short notice. You cannot say this month that you can increase your stock or increase the production of certain farm commodities next month. All farm planning has to be . of a far longer and greater range. It would seem to me that our farmers at the present time are greatly in need of more assurance from the Department of Agriculture

or perhaps I should say from the Minister of Agriculture- of the necessity for maintaining, and the possibility of increasing, or rather the necessity for increasing, food production in the future. We should have surveys made as to the types of food which will be the most cheaply produced in Canada, and therefore the foods which we should concentrate on growing when the war is over. I know that the Department of Agriculture is doing work in this connection but I still feel that there is greater need to bring this information more closely to the farmers to get them to understand. Some people are expressing fear on the question, of making gifts of food after the war is over. Some farmers are even a little dubious as to whether it will be the correct thing for us to do. Here again I believe the Department of Agriculture should show to the farmers how, if the nation as a whole takes on the burden of paying for food to give to other countries, and if at the same time the farmers themselves are guaranteed a fair price, that in itself will be of the greatest good to Canada; because that increased food production with fair prices to the farmers will assure them of being able to buy many things which industry can supply. It will provide employment to the industrial sections of Canada and set a cycle for an increased standard of living throughout the whole of the country.
Generally speaking I would say one of the most important things with regard to agriculture at the present time is to insist on Canada's taking a very strong position on all the boards of the united nations relief and rehabilitation administration and in all matters pertaining to the setting up of trade relations with other food producing countries.
War Appropriation-Agriculture

With regard to our own farmers, I cannot help but emphasize-even though the Minister of Agriculture may be sick of listening to these things which have been stated many times, I do not think we can reiterate them too strongly-the necessity of our farm people having the opportunity to obtain for themselves short term loans and credits through a special agricultural bank, something like the farm security administration in the United States, which has been responsible for such a tremendous increase of food from the smaller types of farms.
Without the shadow of a doubt I believe that our farming people should be guaranteed not only by the federal government but by the provincial governments security of tenure on their land, so that, instead of looking forward only a year or two ahead, they will begin to plan for a long future, in order that the people on the farms can have a stake in the whole rehabilitation programme of Canada in the era of peace.
Undoubtedly the machine problem is a difficult one to solve. In the areas where we have the smaller farming districts which are engaged in mixed farming it is not sufficient for the government to allow a certain quota of machines to be sold. The man who has a farm of a certain size, and the ability to buy a machine, is not always the person who should have it. We would find it of greater value to have certain new machines placed in machinery pools; many farmers would then be in a position to hire a machine, which in many instances could be used on many more farms than a machine purchased by one man. In the smaller mixed farming areas machinery pools and machinery repair depots should be set up under the care of the federal government and its jurisdiction. Repair depots are just as essential as supply depots, because much of the old machinery will still be available. The great difficulty at the present time is the lack of repair centres.
Then there is the question of floors and ceilings on all agricultural products, with a guarantee of at least two or three years in the future. It cannot be denied that that is something which the farmers are seeking before they go into any increased production, particularly of live stock, with any degree of certainty.
The representation of farmers on marketing boards has been dealt with by the two hon. members who preceded me. I can only say that I am in agreement with what they have said. Definitely the farmers themselves are only too anxious to cooperate in all these matters of marketing, but they have in large measure been left out of the discussion on

marketing boards, and for that reason I believe they feel that there are many things in connection with marketing which are not just as they should be. They feel that they have many suggestions to offer which I am sure the Minister of Agriculture would find to be not only to the farmers good but to the general good of agricultural production.
I should like to emphasize-and I believe the minister is in agreement with this-the necessity for the extension of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act to cover the whole of the dominion. In the rehabilitation period, when we have the returned men taking up farming again, and are considering the problem of the best areas for the production of certain kinds of food, I believe there will be the necessity for moving certain of our farmers from submarginal lands and leaving those areas for grazing and reforestation. Our farmers are justified in asking that in the processing of foods there will be more government supervision through greater control of the middleman. Amongst the farmers of western Canada there is resentment because they realize there is an appreciable difference between the prices paid for their raw products and the prices asked for the product which is placed on the market after passing through the hands of one or two middlemen. Definitely there should be an investigation in this sphere to limit or to hold down at least the profits of the middleman. To assure a fair share of the prices to the producer would be something to give satisfaction to the farming people.
I do not feel that any thing should be emphasized more than the necessity for planning and giving to the farmers a clearer understanding of what is to be required of them in the future. The resentment which is still felt-and I urge upon the minister that he realize that this resentment exists in western Canada-is based on the fact that the farmers do not know soon enough ahead of time what is to be required of them. The hesitancy which has been part of their whole attitude toward increased agricultural production would thereby be removed.
When we come to the peace period and thousands of men are being returned to the farms, definitely we should have further provision made for farm labourers. Farm labourers should come under the unemployment insurance provisions, so that we may guarantee to them a definite standard of living and make them feel that their job is to be well paid and recognized as a part of the great industrial development of this country.
These are matters which I believe more than any other are important to the development

War Appropriation-Agriculture
of agriculture. Members who come from agricultural constituencies must take pride in the fact that the production of food and the increased output of agricultural products in Canada will play an important part not only in the winning of the war but also in the stabilization of the peace to follow.

I was interested a few moments ago to listen to the speech of the hon. member for Melfort. He referred to the difference in the price of barley sold on the United States side for ordinary feeding purposes and for malting purposes. Last fall it so happened that nearly all the crop I had for sale in my farm in Manitoba was barley. Inasmuch as the elevators were almost full, and I could not sell very much of it, I obtained export permits from the wheat board to sell my barley on the United States market.
Then, in December, when I was ready to sell it, unfortunately the United States elevators close to my constituency filled up. Since I wished to sell in one quantity all at once, I could not find a place to market it. At that time I believe the bonus for malting barley was between five and ten cents at United States elevators in North Dakota. I was anxious to get that bonus, because it would have meant a considerable profit. However, I was forced to forgo the sale of my barley at that time, and proposed to sell it when I returned during the Easter recess.
At that time I found, after visiting many of the elevators on the United States side, that the .malting bonus had almost disappeared; and by the time I had made my bargain with the elevator there the price was, indeed, $1.20, but there was no bonus for the malting. I visited eight or ten different points in North Dakota, and found that they were uniform in their price, and that there was no bpnus for malting barley. There may have been a time when the facts outlined by the hon. member for Melfort applied. But my barley was sold in the latter part of last month, and the early part of this month, and certainly there was no bonus for malting barley at that time. The United States price of $1.20 prevailed, and that was the top price at the time. I thought the committee should have these facts.

I wish to make a few remarks concerning this war-time appropriation. I would point out to the minister and to the Department of Agriculture that in spite of some of the action taken by the government in a supposed effort to prevent some of the evils of peace-time marketing, a great many of those evils remain. Despite the fact that the producer is receiving a larger return for his product, he is still not receiving the share he should get.
May I give a few cases in point. These are things I had drawn to my attention. Some western farmers who were in a special position to get hold of range cattle and feed them as a special product, found themselves in an awkward situation. They had special feed supplies to last them about ninety days. They brought in Hereford cows from the ranges, and proceeded to fit those animals for market. When the ninety days were up and the animals were ready for sale on the market the farmers were told that the market was glutted, that there was no room for them, that the storage capacity was filled and that the packers could not handle them. The farmers were in desperate circumstances. Their feed supply was gone. It was a matter of continuing to keep the cattle alive by feeding them higher grades of wheat and straw. The farmers were losing money. But the peculiar thing was that, despite the fact that those farmers had been told by the buyers that there was no room on the market for their cattle, other buyers-representatives from the packing plants-offered to buy from the farmers at a cent or a cent and a half a pound below the market price.
Because of their desperate position the farmers sent a delegation to the government at Ottawa. That delegation was assured that after some adjustments the packing plants would take the cows. The fed cows were bought; but the peculiar thing about the transaction was that according to information sent to us later steers were not being accepted at the market price. People who had steers for sale were told exactly the same story, that the packing plants were full and that a sale could not be made. They, too, were offered a cent and a half less a pound for their product.
That type of thing destroys the producers' confidence in the government. It is bringing some to the realization of the fact that so long as the packing industry continues to control the purchase of cattle and other live stock in Canada the farmer can have no hope of any redress, or a proper return for his labour.
Then, too, we had a rather unfortunate circumstance develop on the Winnipeg market within the past year. As in peace time, during these war years there has been a glut of live stock on the market at Winnipeg in the fall. As soon as live stock requires feeding on the farm or in the corral extra labour and expense are involved with the result that farmers usually try to place their live stock on the Winnipeg market early. The result is a fall in price, the farmer taking the loss. By placing floors on farm products, to a certain extent, the government has practically circumvented

War Appropriation-Agriculture
this difficulty. It has introduced regulations whereby it can take over live stock and have it slaughtered if the price falls below a certain level. That however has not cured the situation. The market in Winnipeg became so congested that the packing plants refused to take any more animals.
My information is that something over
140,000	hogs came to the Winnipeg market, and the Winnipeg packing plants could not handle them. The result was that the hogs had to be shipped east, to the Toronto and eastern markets. A terrific loss was suffered, because of the loss of time, the change in feeding, and the necessary delays which occur in shipping, particularly during the winter months.
I would ask the minister, when dealing with this matter, to explain to the committee how the government goes about reimbursing the producer for the loss in grade and price which takes place on these animals. There must be a difference in loss suffered, determined by the number of days required to transfer the animals to the packing plants in the east.
All this naturally leads one to the conclusion that what is needed is orderly marketing, and that proper information should be sent out to the producers respecting the capacity of packing plants and other facilities across the country to take care of production. If there was a shortage of packing space, then the government should and must have known about it. It must have known about this condition, and should have made preparations to meet it. There has been congestion at Winnipeg for some time, -and it still exists.
Here is a farmer who is shipping hogs. He has them fattened, right to the pound, and when he gets them to the market at Winnipeg he finds it is closed. Those hogs hang around for a day or two, and within twenty-four hours they lose their grade. If they have to be shipped back to the farmer, he undergoes a further loss there. Why should the farmer be compelled to take the loss in these cases? Why can there not be some proper adjustment and regulation of the live stock reaching the packing plants so that the animals may be slaughtered at their prime and the greatest possible return made for the farmer? I do not see why the farmer should have to take the loss that results from the fact that facilities are lacking to handle his products. Surely the Department of Agriculture should be able to give information to the shippers at every point, letting them know exactly what is the situation so that they may ship at the very best time.

Last year there was a change in the price of coarse grains being fed to live stock. As the hon. member for Melfort pointed out, this resulted, in the case of a man growing his own grain, in an increase in the cost of producing hogs. As a result many farmers said, "Well, if the government expects us to lose money in producing these hogs we might as well get out of the business," and hundreds of farmers shipped all their hogs, even brood sows, to the market, the consequence being that there was a terrific glut of live stock reaching the Winnipeg slaughtering plants. Farmers were shipping out their brood sows; and figures presented to this house in a return dated February 3 show how the shipment of sows to the Winnipeg market increased. In August, 1943, over 69,000 sows were shipped, as compared with 34,000 in August, 1942; in September, 71,000 were shipped as compared with only 27,000 the year before; in October, 61,000, as compared with 19,000 in 1942, or over three times as many. In November, some
39.000	sows were shipped as compared with
24.000	the year before. At that time an embargo was placed on the shipment of these animals; otherwise I suppose in that month also three times as many sows would have been shipped as the year before. As a matter of fact I believe the embargo is still in effect. In December, 24,000 sows were delivered on the Winnipeg market, as compared with
25.000	the year before. At that time conditions in the stockyards at Winnipeg were terrible; these animals were suffering deterioration in every way, and any sows not accepted were shipped back to the farmers. This should never have happened.

It really did not happen for the reason indicated, either.
Mr. C'ASTLEDEN: Does the minister say that these figures are not correct?
No. I say there were three times as many pigs in Canada last year as in a previous year, so that naturally there would be more sows marketed.
And apparently there were no facilities for handling them.
Yes.
Then why the congestion?
I shall deal with that in a short time.
Canada Packers will tell us all about that.

Yes, Canada Packers will let us know why.
